body.text: These past few weeks have seen mass protests ignite across broad swathes of Europe. From France in the West to Serbia in the East, an extraordinary eruption of activism has transformed the continent into a crucible of protest, a testing ground not for NATO’s latest weapons but for people’s ability to assert their collective power and fight back.

The scale of this continent-wide autumn of discontent is astonishing. Street protests, in many cases youth-led, have unleashed and given form to cross-national outpourings of accumulated frustration and anger. In every sense, these are the wages of austerity. They are the fruit of decades of stagnant wages, underfunded public services, unaddressed needs, destroyed hopes and the wanton waste of human capabilities. Whether the focus of mobilisation is a housing crisis that is pricing people beyond any hope of a decent home (Spain and Portugal), or a crumbling public infrastructure that spells dilapidated classrooms and acute teacher shortages (France), or the threatened return of conscription in goose step with national and European Union militarisation plans (Germany), hundreds of thousands of people across Europe have simply had enough.

That many have taken inspiration from the uprising of French schoolchildren, beginning in mid-September, is evident in the number of education-related protests across the continent. Demonstrations specifically targeted at lamentable school conditions, cuts to higher education and other facets of the war on children and young people have been held in Belgium, Austria, Denmark, Ireland, Greece, Italy, and beyond. Germany’s nationwide mass protests against conscription have also included calls for better higher education funding and relief from rising living costs.

Even where mobilisations have been triggered by specifically local issues (in Albania, for instance, the Trump family’s “development” designs on Sazan Island, whose pristine environment harbours a world-famous flamingo sanctuary), the focus of mass protests has speedily broadened; after all, what does it tell you about a government that’s willing to let key representatives of the global billionaire class seize and despoil an irreplaceable national asset?

One aspect of the developing situation has been the reactivation of the general strike on the continent where it first took shape close to two centuries ago. Over the span of two months, this longstanding weapon of the organised working class has been unsheathed across Europe, especially in Italy, Spain, and France, the three powerful economies at the centre of this ongoing popular revolt.

In Italy, where discontent with the far-right Meloni government is at historic levels, two trade union-sponsored general strikes have been held within the space of four weeks: on October 30 and November 20. On November 11, Spain staged its first general strike since the great Iberian strike of 2012. The previous week, on November 5, tens of thousands of French workers downed tools in a one-day mass strike called by the country’s five main trade union confederations. By the end of the month, the phenomenon was spreading elsewhere: to Greece, for example, where a one-day general stoppage is in progress as I write on November 25.

As its name suggests, the general strike is one that mobilises a significant proportion of workers across a broad swathe of different sectors. Its origins can be traced back to the industrial revolution in Britain, and the concomitant emergence of a new, as yet unorganised, urban proletariat. In the 1840s, working-class anger at the 1832 Reform Act, by whose terms the vast majority of working people were denied the right to vote, crystallised around the Chartist movement and its 1838 list (or charter) of political demands.

In the context of this nascent working-class movement, miners in the Black Country, to the north and west of Birmingham, struck work in May 1842 against proposed wage cuts. The stoppage quickly spread to the Staffordshire potteries and onwards into the mills of Lancashire and Yorkshire. By August, half a million workers had downed tools. Strikers “marched from town to town, from factory to factory, pulling the plugs on furnaces and calling on their fellow workers to join the strike” (Paul Foot, The Vote, 2005: p. 111). The world was witnessing its first general strike.

Soon, cross-sectoral strikes were erupting elsewhere in Europe, and beyond. Addressing the new phenomenon in the first volume of Das Kapital, Marx, who had spoken at a Chartist public meeting in 1848, saw it as contributing to workers’ sense of themselves as, together, constituting “the agent of production”, and to their awareness that if they stopped, then so did production.

But it was the German-Polish Marxist Rosa Luxemburg who, early in the twentieth century, provided the general strike with its most systematic theoretical exploration. Drawing lessons from the 1905 Russian Revolution, which she’d just witnessed at first hand, Luxemburg was struck by the galvanising impact of a series of general strikes in Russia, beginning with the great St. Petersburg textile workers’ strikes of 1896 and 1897. In her tract The Mass Strike (1906), she noted the tendency of strikes involving large-scale industry to develop into directly political struggles; the economic became political and the political economic. Out of this intermingling, there had emerged in Russia a new form of organisation, the soviet or workers’ council, and a plethora of new possibilities.

Twenty years later, in a Europe devastated by war, this potential was put to the test during Britain’s 1926 General Strike, a comprehensive, nine-day, multi-sector stoppage that to this day retains the ability to send shivers down establishment and bourgeois spines. Sparked by private coalmine owners’ bid to impose a wage cut on 1.2 million locked-out pit workers, the strike began as an official one, called (with some reluctance) by the General Council of the Trade Unions Congress (TUC). It was distinguished by the enthusiasm and militancy of its one and a half million participants, which a half-hearted union leadership constantly sought to rein in, and by the no-holds-barred application of state force to crush it: battalions of troops marched through the port city of Liverpool as if for battle, and emergency powers were invoked to give the police multiple new grounds for arrest.

But even this historic rendition of the general strike would be dwarfed by events four decades later when, in May 1968, an estimated ten million French workers, roughly two-thirds of the total workforce, walked off the job, bringing the country’s factories, transportation and public services to a comprehensive halt. Even the considerable repressive powers of the state, at the time being liberally applied to France’s upstart student rebels, were hard put to it to cope with a situation whose gravity and swiftly escalating revolutionary potential at one point drove President Charles de Gaulle to (briefly) flee the country for Germany.

Europe’s current general strikes are taking place in a context far removed from the Trente Glorieuse, the French term for the three post-war decades of economic growth and relative prosperity. With trade union membership in long-term decline, the continent’s depleted ranks of organised labour are seeking new ways to combat the entrenched, life-sapping realities of austerity, authoritarianism and militarisation. There’s a growing emphasis on experimentation, coalition-building and cross-border actions that help foster international perspectives and solidarity.

This new impetus was evident on October 30, when dockworkers from across Europe participated in an international day of action against war, genocide and militarisation. In this global mobilisation of port workers and grass-roots civil society organisations, embracing 22 countries and more than a hundred ports, a key role was played by Italy’s USB (Unione Sindicale di Basa/Unions from the base), a grass-roots, rank-and-file driven trade union confederation with a magnificent record of building solidarity with Palestine.

The significance of this action should not be underestimated. While adapting to new circumstances, the general strike continues to flex its muscles. As mass protests continue across Europe, with zero expectation of any serious response from governments bent on squeezing more from their citizens to feed insatiable military ends, we may, possibly, be at the start of something new: an internationally co-ordinated movement against austerity and war.

Susan Ram has spent much of her life viewing the world from different geographical locations. Born in London, she studied politics and international relations before setting off for South Asia: first to Nepal, and then to India, where fieldwork in Tamil Nadu developed into 20 years of residence.
